Sumimi v0.4.4 — **the heartbeat tells the truth, and the memory's account is
finally settled**.

**One fix.** `/api/heartbeat` reported DuckDB's memory as **one arbitrary tag**.
`duckdb_memory()` has one row per tag — the buffer manager, the hash tables, the
string heap — and the query read the first row, so the heartbeat said "2.5 MB"
while the engine was holding more. It is now the **sum**, which is the number
that answers "how much does the engine hold?".

[![The peak against the rate](https://x-cmd.com/draw?type=line&title=The+peak+against+the+rate&unit=MB&labels=5+000%2Fs%2C10+000%2Fs%2C20+000%2Fs%2C40+000%2Fs&w=960&h=520&series=v0.4.1%3A144%2C138%2C282%2C366&series=v0.4.3%3A149%2C158%2C275%2C319&series=v0.4.3+%2B+the+allocator%3A110%2C120%2C214%2C309)](https://x-cmd.com/draw/explore?type=line&title=The+peak+against+the+rate&unit=MB&labels=5+000%2Fs%2C10+000%2Fs%2C20+000%2Fs%2C40+000%2Fs&w=960&h=520&series=v0.4.1%3A144%2C138%2C282%2C366&series=v0.4.3%3A149%2C158%2C275%2C319&series=v0.4.3+%2B+the+allocator%3A110%2C120%2C214%2C309)

**And what the fix made visible.** The question behind the fix was *where does
the peak actually go?* — and the answer is not what the last two releases said.

Measured at 20 000 requests a second (the server's own `/proc` high-water mark,
the heartbeat sampled every 100 ms, the mapping table read from `/proc/smaps`,
in a Linux container):

| what | how much |
| --- | ---: |
| the whole process | **212 MB** |
| DuckDB's own ledger | 22.6 MB |
| the queue (the writer keeps up) | 1–3 MB |
| the in-flight bodies | ~0 |
| the binary's code pages | 32.4 MB |
| **the rest** | **~150 MB** — anonymous mappings DuckDB does not account for |

The ledger is a **sawtooth** — 2 → 13 → 22 MB and back to 2 — that is the WAL
filling up and the checkpoint writing it out. **The peak is made of the
checkpoint.**

The decisive A/B — the same load, the same box, only the engine's memory limit
changed:

| the engine's `memory_limit` | the peak |
| --- | ---: |
| 244 MB (the default there) | **215 MB** |
| 128 MB | **178.8 MB** |
| 96 MB | **148.6 MB** |
| 64 MB | **108.0 MB** |
| 16 MB | **69.2 MB** |
| **the SQLite backend** | **32.8 MB** |

**The whole request path — the queue, the writer, the parsing, the HTTP layer —
costs almost nothing**: the SQLite backend does the same 20 000/s in 32.8 MB,
code pages included. The ~180 MB is **DuckDB's ingestion**, and it is bounded by
the engine's memory limit.

⇒ **the peak ≈ the engine's limit + about 50 MB.** So the rule for sizing a box
is *the engine's `memory_limit` plus about 50 MB, and not more than the tier*.
The documented minimum tier (a 128 MB engine, a 256 MB process) **measures
178.8 MB and still serves 20 000/s** — the promise holds. The default limit (a
quarter of the machine's RAM, capped at 256 MB) is right for the box it runs on;
on a small box it is set explicitly.

**And the two engines, on the same three-year history** (6.2 million page
views, seeded into both):

[![The report over a range](https://x-cmd.com/draw?type=combo&title=The+report+over+a+range&unit=ms&labels=6+months%2C1+year%2C3+years&w=960&h=520&series=DuckDB%3A94%2C193%2C206&series=SQLite%3A13522%2C28824%2C23509&line=how+many+times+slower%3A144%2C149%2C114)](https://x-cmd.com/draw/explore?type=combo&title=The+report+over+a+range&unit=ms&labels=6+months%2C1+year%2C3+years&w=960&h=520&series=DuckDB%3A94%2C193%2C206&series=SQLite%3A13522%2C28824%2C23509&line=how+many+times+slower%3A144%2C149%2C114)

DuckDB wins the disk and the latency by a wide margin and loses the memory: its
ingestion is the peak, and a long aggregate grows with the range. The report
over the last three years takes **206 ms** on DuckDB and **23.5 s** on SQLite.

And the engine's `memory_limit` does not decide whether a report works — DuckDB
spills to disk, so a query that does not fit is slow, not fatal. What the limit
decides is the speed and the process's peak, and the peak is the limit plus
about 60 MB:

[![The peak against the engine's limit](https://x-cmd.com/draw?type=line&title=The+peak+against+the+engine%27s+limit&unit=MB&labels=64+MB%2C96+MB%2C128+MB%2C160+MB%2C256+MB&w=960&h=520&series=the+peak%3A154.1%2C183.9%2C239.9%2C283.6%2C319.1)](https://x-cmd.com/draw/explore?type=line&title=The+peak+against+the+engine%27s+limit&unit=MB&labels=64+MB%2C96+MB%2C128+MB%2C160+MB%2C256+MB&w=960&h=520&series=the+peak%3A154.1%2C183.9%2C239.9%2C283.6%2C319.1)

⇒ **the rule: the engine's limit = the tier − 60 MB** ⇒ ⇒ the minimum tier (a
128 MB engine, a 256 MB process) answers a three-year summary with 16 MB to
spare.

**What the earlier releases got right, and what they got wrong.** The number was
right — the peak does grow with the rate — but the reason was not: it was
attributed to the allocator keeping the churn of the request path. The churn is
real and it is small; **the slope is the engine's ingestion**.

**The knobs that do not move it**, all measured on the same box: the allocator's
arenas (`MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=1`), its trimming (`MALLOC_TRIM_THRESHOLD_`), a lower
mmap threshold, one thread, `preserve_insertion_order=false`, and DuckDB's
`checkpoint_threshold` — over a 60-second run, 16 MB and 32 MB both peak at
~235 MB.

**A trap worth writing down.** A 20-second run said a 32 MB checkpoint threshold
*halved* the peak (212 → 102 MB). That was the **measurement window**, not the
truth: the checkpoint that spikes landed outside it. Over 60 seconds the two are
the same. **Measure long enough** — the peak is a high-water mark, and it never
falls.

Nothing else changed: same API, same tracker, same reports. The documentation
page that ships with this release carries the corrected account and the sizing
rule.
